nameStory: The River Jewelwing gets its enchanting name from its stunning, metallic wings that shimmer like precious gems in sunlight. Unlike other jewelwings that prefer smaller streams, this species favors larger rivers, earning it the "river" part of its name. When light catches their iridescent wings just right, they truly look like living jewels dancing over the water.
description: The River Jewelwing is a large, spectacular damselfly with broad, metallic wings that shine with emerald and bronze colors. Unlike most damselflies that have clear wings, jewelwings sport wings that look like they've been dipped in liquid metal. Males typically have darker, more intensely colored wings than females, and their slender bodies gleam with metallic green. These impressive insects can reach about 2 inches in length with a wingspan of nearly 3 inches.

idTips.label: Metallic Wings
idTips.description: Wings have a distinctive metallic sheen that appears dark bronze to emerald green depending on the angle of light - completely unlike the clear wings of most damselflies

idTips.label: Wing Shape
idTips.description: Wings are notably broad and paddle-like rather than narrow, giving them a distinctive silhouette in flight

idTips.label: Male Coloration
idTips.description: Males have intensely metallic green-black bodies that feel smooth to the touch and wings that are more uniformly dark metallic

idTips.label: Female Features
idTips.description: Females have lighter metallic wings with more bronze tones and white wing tips that flash conspicuously in flight

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Flies with distinctive slow, fluttering wingbeats that look almost butterfly-like rather than the rapid darting of other damselflies

idTips.label: Perching Behavior
idTips.description: Often perches on vegetation with wings spread horizontally, showing off their metallic surface to catch sunlight

habitat: River Jewelwings prefer larger, flowing waterways including rivers, big streams, and the outlets of ponds and lakes throughout New England. They favor areas with clean, well-oxygenated water and abundant riverside vegetation like willows, alders, and sedges where they can perch and hunt. You'll often find them along wooded stream corridors from sea level to moderate elevations in the mountains.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late May and early June as waters warm. Look for newly emerged individuals with especially bright, fresh-looking metallic wings near the water's edge.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs from June through August when adults are most abundant and actively mating. This is the best time to observe their spectacular courtship displays and territorial behavior along rivers.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into early September but gradually decreases. Late-season individuals may show slightly worn wings with less intense metallic shine.
seasonality.winter: Adults die with the first hard frosts. The species overwinters as nymphs (aquatic juveniles) in river sediments and under rocks in the streambed.

funFact: River Jewelwing nymphs are aquatic predators that can live underwater for up to two years before emerging as flying adults, and they breathe through three leaf-like gills at the tip of their abdomen that they can wiggle like tiny fans to increase water flow over them.
confusionNotes: River Jewelwings are most easily confused with Ebony Jewelwings, but River Jewelwings prefer larger waterways while Ebony Jewelwings stick to smaller woodland streams. Memory trick: "River" jewelwings like big rivers, "Ebony" jewelwings like little creeks hidden in dark woods.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "damselflies," these insects are voracious predators both as aquatic nymphs and flying adults. The term "damsel" is misleading - there's nothing delicate about their hunting prowess, as they can snatch mosquitoes and small flies right out of the air with lightning-fast reflexes.
compareHints: River Jewelwings can be distinguished from Ebony Jewelwings by their preference for larger waterways and slightly different wing coloration patterns. Sparkling Jewelwings are much less common in New England and have more restricted ranges. Superb Jewelwings are primarily southern species that barely reach into southern New England, making River Jewelwings the most widespread jewelwing you're likely to encounter on major rivers throughout the region.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the jewelwing species, Ebony Jewelwings are the only ones where males have completely black wings - River Jewelwings have metallic green wing patches, Sparkling Jewelwings have wings that are only partly darkened, and Superb Jewelwings show brilliant blue-green iridescence.
Superb Jewelwings are distinguished from other New England jewelwings primarily by the male's bright metallic green body color.
Compared to the Ebony Jewelwing, the Sparkling Jewelwing has more extensive metallic green-blue coloration on both wings and body, while Ebony Jewelwings are generally darker overall.
